blocks.text: A file descriptor is a small non-negative integer indexing the process's fd table. The kernel resolves that integer to an open file description.

items: Every process starts with `0` stdin, `1` stdout, `2` stderr.
Redirection never edits the program — it repoints fds before `exec`.
Programs write to numbers: `printf` calls `write(1, ...)`.
fd 1 may be a tty, a file or a pipe — the program cannot tell.
The description holds offset, open flags and status.
Two fds can share one description; each `open` makes a new one.
Shared description = shared write position.
That is why `>&` differs from opening the same file twice.

blocks.title: Why Colour Vanishes
blocks.text: `[ -t 1 ]` is the idiom behind tools that auto-disable colour once stdout is a pipe.

lines: exec 3< data.txt   # persistent fd 3, whole shell

items: Bash lets you name fds `0`-`9` for user redirection.
`{fd}<` writes the free number into `$fd` — no collisions.

blocks.title: Not A Builtin
blocks.text: `>` is a syntactic operator processed before the command is even located, not a builtin acting on a command.

lines: cmd 2 > err.log     # BUG: '2' is an argument
# several results, one pass over the data

items: Descriptors survive `fork` unconditionally.
They survive `exec` too unless marked close-on-exec.
Bash sets close-on-exec on its own bookkeeping fds.
It does NOT on your `exec 3<` — children inherit fd 3.
`>>` seeks to end atomically — small concurrent appends stay intact.
`< file` needs the file to exist; it never creates one.
`<>` suits device files and read-modify-write on fixed-size files.
The digit must touch the operator: `2>` not `2 >`.
`&> f` and `>& f` are Bash shorthand for `> f 2>&1`.
`&>> f` appends both streams.
Neither is POSIX — write the long form in `sh` scripts.
The shell opens the target before the command runs.
`> out.txt` truncates even if the command does not exist.
Redirections run left-to-right, after expansion, before exec.
`> out.txt echo hi` equals `echo hi > out.txt`.

lines: echo x > have.txt   # cannot overwrite existing file

blocks.title: The File Eater
blocks.text: `sort file > file` destroys the file: the shell truncates it before `sort` reads a byte. Use a temp file or `sponge`.
`n>&m` duplicates: fd n becomes a copy of fd m, both pointing at one open file description. It is a `dup2(m, n)` call.

items: `/dev/null` swallows writes, reads as EOF.
`cmd > /dev/null 2>&1` is the standard silence idiom.
Bash-only: `> /dev/tcp/host/port` and `/dev/udp/...` open sockets.
`/dev/fd/N` names a descriptor that is already open.

blocks.title: Say It Out Loud
blocks.text: `2>&1` means: send stderr wherever stdout points RIGHT NOW. It copies a target, it does not create a lasting alias.

items: `> file 2>&1`: stdout moves first, stderr copies the new target.
`2>&1 > f`: stderr copies the terminal, then stdout leaves.
The second form is almost always a bug.
Redirections mutate the fd table one step at a time.

lines: # 2 joins the pipe, then 1 is discarded

items: `n>&-` closes fd n; `n<&-` closes it for reading.
Writing to a closed fd raises `EBADF`, not silence.
`n<&m` is input-side duplication.
`read line <&3` reads the fd from `exec 3< file`.
`|&` is Bash shorthand for `2>&1 |`.
The pipe is wired before the command's own redirections.
So `2>&1` inside a pipeline sees the pipe as stdout's target.

blocks.title: xtrace Plumbing
items: `exec 2> trace.log; set -x` files the trace stream.
`BASH_XTRACEFD=5` diverts trace without touching stderr.
Keeps program stderr readable while tracing.

blocks.text: `cmd <<EOF ... EOF` feeds the literal block to stdin. Bash writes the body to a temp file or pipe and attaches it to fd 0.

lines: echo "$line" | read a b   # subshell, lost

items: Unquoted: `$HOME`, `$(date)`, arithmetic and escapes all fire.
Quote it for AWK programs, scripts, anything holding `$`.
`<<-` strips TABs only — never spaces.
That lets you indent a heredoc inside a function or loop.

blocks.title: Terminator Alone
blocks.text: The delimiter needs its own line with no trailing whitespace. One stray space and Bash reports `unexpected end of file`.

items: `<<< "text"` is a one-line heredoc.
The word is expanded and a trailing newline added.
Idiomatic field split with no subshell.

lines: cat 3<<EOF   # block lands on fd 3, not stdin

items: `<<` and `>` order does not matter — different fds.
Several heredocs on one line queue in delimiter order.
Bodies start after the whole command line ends.

blocks.title: Where It Runs Out
items: One blocking chunk of literal text — no streaming.
Cannot be regenerated; dynamic data wants a pipe.
Inner `while read` eats the lines the outer loop needed.

blocks.text: `a | b` calls `pipe()` for a kernel buffer, forks both commands, dup2s the write end onto a's fd 1 and the read end onto b's fd 0, then closes the spare ends.

items: Both sides run concurrently, not one after the other.
Buffer is finite — 64 KiB on Linux by default.
Full buffer blocks the writer; empty one blocks the reader.
That mutual blocking is the flow control.

lines: yes | head -1   # head exits, read end closes

items: Only stdout travels the pipe by default.
stderr still hits the terminal unless you add `2>&1`.
`|&` sends both streams into the next stage.

lines: echo x | read v; echo $v   # prints nothing
shopt -s lastpipe          # last stage in this shell

items: Each stage runs in its own subshell.
Assignments in the last stage vanish by default.
`lastpipe` needs non-interactive shell, job control off.
Pipeline status is the LAST command's status only.
`PIPESTATUS` holds every stage's status as an array.
The very next command overwrites it — copy immediately.

blocks.title: Splitting And Naming
items: `cmd | tee log.txt | grep err` files and continues.
`tee /dev/tty` peeks at data mid-pipeline.
Pipes are anonymous; `mkfifo` puts one in the filesystem.
A FIFO lets unrelated processes connect.

blocks.text: Bash creates a pipe (or FIFO), forks cmd on one end, and passes `/dev/fd/N` of the other end as an ordinary argument.

items: A pipe can only feed one thing: stdin.
Process substitution supplies many streams as arguments.
`<(cmd)` substitutes a FILENAME that reads cmd's output.
On Linux that path looks like `/dev/fd/63`.
`>(cmd)` substitutes a filename that feeds cmd's stdin.

lines: # two live outputs, zero temp files
while read l; do n=$((n+1)); done \
find . -type f | while read l; do :; done  # lost

blocks.title: The Mandatory Space
blocks.text: Write `< <(...)` with a space. `<<(` is parsed as a here-document operator instead.

lines: # each stream to its own consumer

items: The path is a pipe — not seekable, `lseek` consumers fail.
`sort -m` or `tar` on tape can need a re-read and break.
The shell does not wait for `>(cmd)`; add an explicit `wait`.
Its exit status reaches neither `$?` nor `PIPESTATUS`.
Not POSIX — Bash, ksh and zsh only.
`sh script.sh` on dash: `Syntax error: "(" unexpected`.
No `/dev/fd`? Bash falls back to FIFOs in `/tmp`.
That changes cleanup and permission behaviour.

lines: echo $?   # 0 — tar succeeded on empty input

items: pipefail flattens detail; `PIPESTATUS` keeps per-stage truth.
`set -o pipefail` in a function persists after it returns.
Save and restore, or wrap in `( set -o pipefail; ... )`.
`$?` holds the last foreground command's status.
`0` is success; `1`-`255` are failures.
`128+N` means killed by signal N.
`143` = SIGTERM, `141` = SIGPIPE.
By default a pipeline reports only its last stage.
`set -o pipefail` returns the rightmost NON-ZERO status.
It returns zero only when every stage succeeded.
`set -e` aborts the script when a command fails.
It stays silent in `if`, `while`, `&&`, `||` and `!` contexts.
It does not catch pipeline failures either.
`set -u` errors on unset vars — kills `rm -rf $DIR/`.

blocks.title: pipefail Bites Head
blocks.text: `cmd | head -1` now fails: head exits early, cmd dies of SIGPIPE with status 141. Wrap or filter that case explicitly.

lines: set -E   # functions inherit the ERR trap

blocks.title: Deliberate Swallow
blocks.text: `cmd || true` intentionally ignores a failure under `set -e`. Write it on purpose, never by accident.

lines: cmd1 > out.txt; cmd2 >> out.txt  # two opens
while read l; do echo "$l"; done < in.txt
myfn() { date; } > log   # every call site

items: Loop redirection opens the file once and streams it.
A redirect on the definition attaches at every invocation.
Subshells inherit the parent fd table as it stands.

lines: exec 3>&1 > file      # save old stdout in 3

items: Everything after the bare `exec` is logged.
`exec cmd` WITH a command replaces the shell process.
Same PID, no fork, no code after it ever runs.

blocks.title: The Stdin Thief
blocks.text: `ssh` or `ffmpeg` inside a `while read` loop eats the loop's stdin. Add `< /dev/null` to the inner command, or read the loop from fd 3.

blocks.note: ssh cannot eat the loop's fd 3

blocks.title: Two-Way Wiring
items: `coproc` backgrounds a command with both ends wired.
`${COPROC[0]}` reads it, `${COPROC[1]}` writes to it.
Useful for a running conversation with one process.

blocks.title: Coarse By Design
blocks.text: Block redirection is cheap but blunt: one failing command inside `{ }` writes to the same log. Per-stage tagging needs separate redirects.

items: Duplication copies the CURRENT target, so order rules everything.
`sort f > tmp && mv tmp f` works for tools without `-o`.
Two opens make two independent offsets that overwrite.
Process substitution also keeps the read out of a subshell.

lines: cmd 2 > file    # stdout redirected, '2' an argument

items: An unquoted heredoc delimiter mangles `$var` and backticks.
Quote it as `<<'EOF'` whenever the body must stay literal.
Trailing whitespace after the terminator: `unexpected end of file`.
`<<-` with space indentation strips nothing — TABs only.

blocks.text: sudo Does Not Own The Redirect

lines: sudo echo x > /root/f   # your shell opens it: denied
echo x | sudo tee /root/f   # tee runs as root

blocks.note: any command in between resets PIPESTATUS

slides.page_title: The Whole Manual on One Page

items: Unclosed `exec 3<` leaks fds; long loops hit `EMFILE`.
`>(cmd)` output may be incomplete when the script exits.
Add `wait` before you read what the writer produced.

blocks.title: Portability Check
blocks.text: `cmd &> file` under `#!/bin/sh` is not portable. Write `> file 2>&1` and it runs anywhere.

items: Redirection rewires the arrow at the FIRST hop only.
It all happens before the command runs, strictly left to right.
That single rule explains `2>&1 > file` completely.

blocks.q: Why does a broken pipeline report success?
a_bullets: `$?` carries only the last stage's status.
Reading `PIPESTATUS` after any command shows THAT command.

caption.text: `2>&1 > file` and `> file 2>&1` look like the same command typed in a different mood — one files both streams, the other leaves stderr on your terminal. This 10-page field manual walks the fd table from `dup2` up through heredocs, process substitution and `pipefail`, so you can read any redirection left to right and know exactly where every byte goes. Save it for the next time a cron job swears it succeeded.
